label: Kimi K3.1 Pro
output:
D. Bergeron, you’re right about one thing: people deserve a straight answer, and I should have given one before the rumours started. So here it is.

**We are not closing. We are not moving. The carnets are still good. And the “grande nouvelle” is that I have bought the building.**

I had wanted to keep that last part a surprise until the reopening, but so much for my surprise. I would rather tell you now than have people worry for another day.

M. Ferland, who owns the building, is 81 and is retiring to Sherbrooke to be with his daughter. He offered to sell it to me before offering it to anyone else, and we signed at the notary on December 15. It still feels a little strange to write “I bought the building,” but it is true: the bakery, the ground floor and the three apartments upstairs.

Marc-Antoine, your cousin had part of the story right. The building was sold. It was sold to me. I understand why a sale on that corner would make people fear condos, a bank or a vape shop, because we have all seen versions of that story in Mile End. But this time, the ending is different. The little bakery at 5 Fairmount is staying.

And since people are worried about the building, I want to reassure the tenants upstairs too: **the three apartments will stay rented, with the same tenants and the same rent. I have promised them that in writing.** Buying the building is not a plan to push people out of their homes.

The closure from January 4 to January 18 is for work in the bakery. We are getting a new four-deck oven, coming from a supplier in Laval. Our present oven dates from 1998 and has broken down three times this year. Anyone who has arrived on one of those mornings to find me apologizing instead of taking bread out of the oven will understand why this is necessary. We are also taking the space at the back, the old storage space of the dépanneur. There will be six small tables, so people will finally be able to sit down instead of balancing a coffee and a croissant on the sidewalk.

**We will reopen on Tuesday, January 19, at 7 a.m.**

Now, about the carnets, because this is the part I want to make completely clear.

We sold **214 carnets in October**, at **$60 for 12 loaves**. Every one of them remains valid, in full. **There is no expiry date.** The two weeks of work do not cancel anything, reduce anything or change the agreement. If you have seven loaves left, you still have seven loaves. If you have not started using yours, all twelve are waiting for you.

In January, **each carnet holder will also receive one free croissant**, as a small thank-you for your trust and your patience.

And if somebody truly does not feel comfortable and would prefer their money back, come and see me. **I will refund the carnet, no questions asked.** You do not have to argue with me or explain yourself. I would much rather return the money than have someone feel that I took advantage of them.

To noodle_and_crumb: I understand that the timing looked bad from outside. You paid in October, then saw a closed sign in December without an explanation. I am not angry at you for raising it. But I hope you can see now that this was not money collected before disappearing. Those loaves are yours, and I intend to bake every single one of them.

The sign itself was my mistake. My nephew Thomas wrote it at six in the morning, and “grande nouvelle” was his idea. He was excited, and I said yes without thinking enough about how it would sound to somebody reading it on the door. “Closed” together with “big news soon” was supposed to mean renovations and something to celebrate. I can see now that it could just as easily sound like a vague goodbye. That is on me, not on Thomas. Mr. Bergeron, when you say that a two-week vacation does not require a “big news soon,” you are being fair. This was never just a vacation notice badly disguised; it was the oven, the back room and the building. I simply should have explained it properly.

The shelves were another unfortunate detail. They looked half empty on the 28th because we had sold everything for Christmas Eve, including **400 bûches**. It had nothing to do with closing. After 17 years, I suppose I should be used to the shop looking a little stripped after the Christmas rush, but I understand how the sign, the bare shelves and the rumour of a sale all added up to something frightening.

And since I am being honest, the word “scam” hurt. I understand the worry. Mile End has lost too many small shops, and people are not wrong to be suspicious when money has changed hands and information is missing. I am not going to pretend I enjoyed reading that word, though, after working here since March 2009. Seventeen years on the same street, learning people’s names, watching their children grow up, and finding out how they like their bread — that is why it stung.

M. Ferland has come nearly every morning for those same 17 years for his *baguette pas trop cuite*. He cried a little at the notary. This place has meant something to him for a long time, and it means something to me too. I did not buy the building so I could close it.

Priya, thank you for defending me, and for remembering the chocolatines. Thank you as well to everyone else who spoke up for us, sent a kind word, or simply waited to hear my side before deciding. I am very grateful.

Jules, you are not losing your pain de campagne.

Please consider this my official invitation: after we reopen on January 19, **come celebrate with us on Saturday, January 23**. Everyone is welcome — regulars, carnet holders, neighbours, the upstairs tenants, and yes, the people who were worried or skeptical too. **Coffee and a piece of the new bread will be free.** Come see the changes, sit at one of the little tables, and let me thank you in person.

I am sorry that my badly worded sign caused all this anxiety. But I am happy that I can finally give you the real news: we are staying, and I hope to be baking on this corner for many years to come.

Hélène  
Boulangerie Le Pétrin Doré
